clinicalPearls: Deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor causes recurrent, non-pruritic, non-urticarial angioedema of skin, gut and airway mediated chiefly by bradykinin.
Type I (about 85 percent) shows low antigenic and functional C1-INH, whereas type II shows normal or high antigenic levels with reduced function.
A persistently low C4 between and during attacks is a useful screening clue; confirmation requires C1-INH antigenic and functional assays.
Attacks are self-limiting over 2 to 5 days but laryngeal involvement can be fatal from asphyxiation.
Abdominal attacks mimic a surgical abdomen with colic, vomiting and ascites, frequently leading to unnecessary laparotomy.
Triggers include trauma, dental work, oestrogens, ACE inhibitors and emotional stress; lesions do not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline.
Acute treatment uses C1-INH concentrate, a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist or a kallikrein inhibitor; prophylaxis employs C1-INH, attenuated androgens or a plasma kallikrein inhibitor.
Acquired C1-INH deficiency, associated with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease, features low C1q and later onset without family history.
reference.pathophysiology: C1 inhibitor is a serine protease inhibitor that regulates the classical complement pathway, the contact (kallikrein-kinin) system, the coagulation cascade and fibrinolysis. In hereditary angioedema, autosomal dominant mutations in SERPING1 reduce the quantity (type I) or function (type II) of C1-INH. Loss of inhibition permits unchecked activation of plasma kallikrein, generating excess bradykinin from high-molecular-weight kininogen. Bradykinin acts on endothelial B2 receptors to increase vascular permeability, producing localised subcutaneous and submucosal oedema. Consumption of C4 and C2 through unregulated classical pathway activity explains the characteristically low C4.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency with lymphoproliferative disease
Hereditary angioedema with normal C1-INH (factor XII or plasminogen mutations)
additionalInvestigations: Serum C4 level (low during and between attacks)
C1q level to distinguish acquired from hereditary forms
SERPING1 gene sequencing when diagnosis is uncertain
Screening for underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder in suspected acquired disease
redFlags: Laryngeal oedema with voice change, dysphagia or stridor threatening the airway
Rapidly progressive facial or neck swelling
Severe abdominal attack with hypovolaemia from third-space fluid loss
First presentation of angioedema in an older adult suggesting acquired deficiency and occult malignancy
Failure of swelling to respond to adrenaline, antihistamine and corticosteroid
reference.prognosis: With modern on-demand and prophylactic therapy most patients achieve good control and a normal life expectancy, but untreated laryngeal attacks carry a significant mortality. Disease severity and attack frequency vary widely even within a single family.
pitfalls: Treating bradykinin-mediated angioedema as an allergic reaction with adrenaline, steroids and antihistamines, which are ineffective.
Proceeding to laparotomy for recurrent abdominal attacks misdiagnosed as a surgical emergency.
Prescribing ACE inhibitors or oestrogen-containing contraceptives, which precipitate attacks.
Relying on a single normal C4 to exclude the diagnosis, since it is most reliably low during an attack.
Overlooking acquired C1-INH deficiency by not checking C1q in late-onset disease.
references: Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice, current edition
